spec.title: Cut-over: the mode flag, shadow and parity, going active, rollback, retiring the watchers
spec.purpose: The scheduler replaces the bash belt behind a flag: it runs beside the belt, deciding without acting, until its decisions match the belt's for enough records, then takes the belt's state and place; the flag is the way back.

section.title: What the cut-over domain decides

node.title: Cut-over: shadow beside the bash belt until parity holds for the configured number of records, then active with the watcher panes stopped and the ledger adopted; rollback is the mode flag and the panes back

section.text: In: the mode, the shadow directory, the bash belt's state directory and receipts. Out: the gate on the job runner, the shadow decision files, the parity report, the runbook steps.

section.title: The mode flag
section.text: off: the scheduler answers health and status and does nothing else. shadow: it decides and writes decisions, runs only observation verbs. active: it decides and acts. The key is a variable, so the pane wrapper sets it from the environment.
The job runner checks the mode before every Run: in shadow a mutating verb is never sent and the job is written to the shadow directory as decided; in off no job is created at all.
Observation verbs: agent_list, pane_read, pane_process_info, seat_quiet. Every other verb mutates.

section.title: Shadow mode
section.text: Shadow uses its own state directory: its own boundary, ledger, jobs and belt. It never reads or writes the bash belt's state, so the two run side by side on the same log.

For every record intake lists, one decision file in the shadow directory named by the record id: the plan, the escalation count used, the table version, and every job it would have run with verb and arguments.
Policies decide in shadow too: a default the scheduler would apply is a decision file naming the policy and the escalation, compared with the policy watch's policy.applied records.
Health judges in shadow and logs its verdicts; it writes no note and shows no notification.

section.title: The parity report
section.text: The oracle is the bash belt: for each decision file, the bash ledger's word for that id, and when it says done, the receipt record the bash runner wrote naming the id. The report compares verdict, action, addressee and down.
The receipt's note is parsed here and nowhere else in the scheduler: it is the bash runner's fixed format, read by a report tool, and the parity ticket's test pins the format with a fixture.

The report lists every mismatch with both sides and exits 0 only when the records compared reach the configured minimum and mismatches are zero; otherwise 1. Going active is refused by the runbook while it exits 1.

Known, accepted differences are not mismatches: the scheduler holds and retries where the belt wrote a 500; the report shows them as a separate count, improvements, with the bash 500 note beside the scheduler's job.

section.title: Going active
section.text: By the runbook, in order: parity exits 0; the three belt panes and two architect watches are released through the monitors script; the state directory key points at the belt's; mode active; pane restarted; status says active.
Adopting the bash state directory means the ledger, the boundary and the belt file continue: a record the belt routed is never routed again, and the first unrouted record is the scheduler's first.

The belt status command in the herdr configuration becomes the scheduler's status with the belt flag, and the runner slot's command becomes the scheduler wrapper; the executor takes a slot the released watches held.
The window between the belt stopping and the scheduler going active is one restart of one pane; records written in it are routed when the scheduler ticks, because the ledger is shared.

section.title: Rollback
section.text: Mode off, restart the pane, restore the slot and belt status commands, run bring-up: the belt panes come back on the shared ledger and route from the first record the scheduler had not finished. Every claim is a file; nothing is lost.
Jobs the scheduler had in flight are left in its store; a record it claimed but did not finish is interrupted for the belt, which reports it once, as it does for its own.

section.title: Retiring the bash watchers
section.text: Retired at cut-over: the route runner, flow watch, policy watch, gate record watch and seat turn watch (each a released grid slot) and the interim copies in the user cache; the scripts stay as the parity oracle until a ticket removes them.
After cut-over the architect is woken only by rows: a merged record to verify, an escalation to re-scope. No watch prompts it for every gate record or every finished turn; the line runs without it.

section.title: Acceptance
section.text: First in a scratch herdr session with a stub agent: a pr.opened written into the log is routed to a seated tester with no bash watcher running, receipt and ledger word match the fixtures, and the tester's down follows its test.passed.
Then on the live session for one real pull request: the same path, with the belt panes released, observed in status and in the two panes; that run is the epic's acceptance.

section.title: Keys this domain reads
section.key: How many compared records parity needs before it may exit 0.
The shadow's own in shadow mode; the bash belt's when active.

section.title: Cases the build ticket proves

case.expected: exit 0: over the replay fixtures in shadow the fake executor saw only observation verbs and one decision file exists per record
exit 0: a fixture bash state directory with receipts yields zero mismatches for agreeing decisions and names each disagreeing one with both sides
exit 0: below the minimum records or with a mismatch the report exits 1, otherwise 0

section.case: The runbook can gate on it.

case.expected: exit 0: started active on a bash state directory the scheduler routes nothing already ledgered and routes the first unrouted record
tests: N passed, 0 failed: in the scratch herdr session a pr.opened routes to a seated stub tester with no bash pane present

example.text: Parity over 300 records: 297 agree, 3 are improvements where the belt wrote a 500 for a refused bring-up and the scheduler holds a retry; zero mismatches; the operator goes active.
Going active with the route runner pane still running.
example.why: Two routers on one ledger race on every claim; one of them reports every record as interrupted.

example.text: Shadow mode writing its belt into the bash belt's file to keep the supervisor quiet.
example.why: The supervisor would see a moving belt with no runner behind it.
